title: Cultivation No-Dig
site: Imagined first spring on John's newly taken-over allotment. A single starter bed is reclaimed in fallow grass beside the trodden path. The faded mint-green shed is reconstructed with weathered boards.

joint_render.prompt:
Photorealistic three-step horticultural documentary sequence for John Lennon's The Vegetable Guru, UK. New matched photographic triptych, FULL BLEED EXACTLY THREE EQUAL SQUARE FRAMES in a horizontal row. Entire deliverable 3:1 wide by high (2172 x 724 or larger). Two clean butt joins at one third and two thirds, no shared subjects crossing the joins, no borders, no lettering of any kind. Three photographs of the SAME ONE BED, SAME CLOTHES, same spot, taken minutes apart on one cool spring afternoon. Show the small first patch reclaimed from a NEGLECTED, OVERGROWN CORNISH ALLOTMENT where there were NO cultivated beds. Teach real no-dig technique. Four photographic references are supplied with intentionally different jobs.

THE FACE IS CRITICAL. Reference 1 consists of three actual unretouched camera crops of the same man looking down at work. Use his real face from these photos directly, not a new generic bearded middle-aged man. Use the FIRST (left-facing, near-profile) face pose, camera slightly above, for at least the first shot; use the middle and right for the other two as his gaze follows his hands. Literally follow the silhouette from lower lip into CHIN as it sweeps diagonally back TOWARDS THE THROAT: the chin is small and notably RECEDING, well behind the projecting lower lip; at this downwards working angle the underside of the chin is foreshortened into the collar. Preserve natural nose (forward-most feature), lip position, short softly greying close beard. The short grey hairs lie close to this actual small tucked jaw and don't extend it. No squaring, adding a projecting chin-pad, thick beard extension, strong broad jaw, or carving a dramatic jawline. Match actual shape of ears, forehead, cheeks, relaxed gaze, age, clothing. Maintain same man's build and consistent head/shoe size in all three. His usual olive knitted cap, teal fleece, dark rib knit jumper collar, blue jeans, working boots from refs 1 and 3. No microphone. Hands gentle, natural real working postures.

Reference 2 is purely for the plot geography: man's plot LEFT of main path looking toward his pale mint-green timber shed. Reference 3 verifies shed shape and man’s size and wardrobe only. RECONSTRUCT THE WHOLE FOREGROUND AND BACKGROUND as an early day on this freshly taken-over plot. No existing rows of vegetables, cultivated beds, raked soil, smart borders, closely mown lawns, weed membranes, gleaming sheds or ordered allotment furniture. From foreground into distance, coarse uneven tussock grass with last year's bent straw-coloured stems, nettles and dock mixed into FAR margins, closer buttercups and dandelion/plantain rosettes embedded in real sprawling mixed sward; small patches of earth between grass. Ragged, clumpy, in drifts, not planted or artificially distributed. The only route is a narrow muddy/flattened, trodden grassy track to the right, physically clear of the bed. In the distance see just part of the same recognisable pale green shed, old, faded uneven mint, pale grey timber showing through the paint along low shiplap courses, weather-stained sill and roof felt, modest local wear from Cornish weather. Preserve actual form and colour identity. It stands quietly at the back as the only recognisable manmade landmark. Do not include the neighbour's brown shed. Shed should read as old at small book size, still standing and usable. Permanent landmarks and distinctive tussocks stay in precisely the same place in all three, same daylight, same footprint registered to the same trampled path. Outside the one bed, ALL the unmanaged weeds remain visibly undisturbed in ALL THREE pictures. No extensive clearing of the surroundings between shots. Inside the proposed bed grass and soft nonwoody weeds bent or roughly scythed short enough to put cardboard directly on top. No woody plants under the cardboard. Bed footprint a modest irregular-edged 1 x 2 m shape in the grass to left of track. Work exclusively from the path to the right.

Reference 4 (three documentary views from a DIFFERENT garden) shows genuine cardboard and mature compost texture only; omit its stone edging, greenhouse, furniture and built surroundings. Camera same 3/4 view from near right-hand corner of bed, modestly elevated standing photographer looking across and down. Tight practical shot: foreground bed fills left two thirds of each square, person at right, hands and work clearly read when printed 45 mm across. Show enough downturned face to read real receding profile against a quiet patch. See wild grass behind and along long LEFT and far edges in each photo so the transformation is obvious. Do not let the clean area expand into the rest of the plot. Natural spring light, Cornwall magazine documentary photos with honest imperfect texture and clothing, useful not posed.

LEFT: JOHN IS MAKING THE FIRST INCURSION INTO THE OVERGROWTH. John kneels from the trodden path, head dipped as in actual reference 1. He is laying/pressing a large plain brown torn-open cardboard box flat OVER flattened grass, partly overlapping the other plain sheet by a generous handspan, no tape or printing. Only the near HALF of the proposed new bed is covered at this instant. CLEARLY SEE a substantial part of the SAME future bed still full of coarse green grass and broadleaf rosettes up to/under the loose edge of the sheet he is laying. Let a few bent blades stick from beneath the cardboard. No visible pre-existing bed border or black earth. Uneven fallow grass must be conspicuous rather than a neatly delineated rectangle of weeds.
MIDDLE: SAME exact location, now most of those overlapping cardboard sheets covered right from near to far with around 4 inches of dark, mature, crumbly compost. Leave one small patch of brown cardboard visible just beyond the unfinished compost. From the adjacent path John gently levels the compost with a plain straight-handled garden rake; turn the rake so the smooth BACK is against the compost and the tines point up, correctly attached in the middle of the head, normal proportions. The new bed edge gently slopes into the tussocky surroundings, no edging. A natural relaxed stance, eyes following the work. 
RIGHT: Newly finished SAME soft-sided bed, all cardboard covered, loose flat compost. Kneeling on that same rough path, one hand places a single small young lettuce plug at its original pot depth, other hand rests a small trowel by the freshly opened hole. Three or four other young lettuces already in, sensibly spaced, easy to distinguish from the weeds OUTSIDE. John's upper body in a quietly intent posture, head down with real soft chin tucked back under mouth, accurate from reference. WEEDY unworked grass immediately surrounds the bed, same tuft landmarks as panel 1. Keep the camera, path, shed, lens, corners and body size registered in all 3 frames. No timelapse growth of crops. No captions, montage within panels or graphics.

likeness_note: John describes a quite receding chin. Use the photographed lower-lip-to-chin silhouette in the April 2026 working views, particularly when his head is lowered and the camera looks down. The beard stays close to the jaw. Confirm likeness with John.
same_day_wardrobe: Match the olive knit hat, teal fleece, jumper and jeans visible in the April allotment footage.
